screens.title: Optimizing Scripting & C# Code
screens.subtitle: Make your game logic run smoothly by reducing allocations, caching wisely, and reusing objects.

narration.text: In this chapter we'll focus on practical patterns that stop your C# scripts from becoming the largest cause of frame hitches. You'll learn the why and the how for object pooling, which prevents frequent instantiation and destruction during gameplay. We will also study common allocation pitfalls — string concatenation, boxing, LINQ, temporary collections, and coroutines — and show how small changes reduce garbage collector pauses. You will see strategies to optimize both Update and FixedUpdate loops: caching references once, using event-driven designs, and lowering update frequency when possible. Finally, we'll review expensive Unity A P I calls like GetComponent, Camera. main, and Find methods, and describe safe alternatives for production builds. Each topic includes concrete code examples and a small hands-on activity so you can measure the improvement in the Profiler. By the end of the lesson you'll be able to explain why allocations create GC spikes, implement a reliable object pool for fast-spawning objects, and refactor a heavy Update loop to be both correct and efficient. Consider a gameplay scenario where bullets spawn hundreds per second — that will become the running example for why these patterns matter.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Reduce allocations, reuse objects, and cache references to eliminate CPU spikes and make gameplay smoother.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Overview
screens.subtitle: Four essential skills to write efficient Unity C# scripts.

narration.text: These objectives guide your practical work in the chapter. First, you'll implement object pooling to avoid costly instantiate and destroy cycles. Object pooling matters when you spawn many short-lived objects, such as bullets or particles, because it prevents repeated memory allocation and reduces garbage collector interruptions. Second, you'll learn to minimize garbage collection allocations by recognizing common sources: string concatenation, boxing, LINQ in hot paths, and per-frame allocations. Understanding these pitfalls helps you spot GC spikes in the Profiler. Third, you'll optimize Update and FixedUpdate loops by caching references, reducing frequencies, and switching to event-driven or timer-based updates when possible. This saves C P U time every frame. Fourth, you'll apply best practices for Unity A P I calls: avoid repeated GetComponent and Find operations, cache Camera. main and other commonly used objects, and prefer serialized or injected references in production code. Each objective includes a small code example and a verification milestone so you can confirm the improvement in the Profiler. As you work through the activities, ask yourself: where does your code allocate per frame, and can that allocation be moved or eliminated?

screens.title: Object Pooling — Definition & Rationale
screens.subtitle: Why pooling matters and how it reduces runtime cost.

narration.text: Object pooling is a design pattern where a set of objects is pre-allocated and reused rather than created and destroyed repeatedly at runtime. In games this often applies to bullets, particle effects, enemies, or UI elements that appear and disappear frequently. The performance cost we avoid comes from repeated memory allocation and subsequent garbage collection; instantiating an object often allocates memory, and destroying it later forces the garbage collector to reclaim that memory, creating potential frame hitches. A pool instead keeps inactive objects in a collection, such as a queue, list, or stack. When the game needs an instance, it borrows one, resets its state, and activates it. When the object is no longer needed, it is deactivated and returned to the pool. Concretely, a pool implemented as a Queue will Enqueue deactivated items at creation or return time and Dequeue when needed. A misconception is that pooling is only for extreme cases. In reality, any gameplay element that spawns frequently benefits from pooling because the GC overhead compounds over many frames. Key takeaway: pool when instantiation frequency causes measurable allocations in the Profiler, and always match pool size and reset logic to your game's lifecycle so objects don't retain unwanted state.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Pool objects to reuse memory and avoid costly Instantiate/Destroy patterns that drive GC spikes.

content.html:
Core Concept › Object Pooling
What is object pooling?
A reusable collection of pre-allocated objects that you borrow and return instead of instantiating and destroying.
How it works:
  • Pre-allocate a set of objects at level start and keep them inactive.
  • When needed, activate an object and reset its state.
  • When finished, deactivate it and return it to the pool.
Common misconception
Pooling is only for extreme cases. In practice, many moderate spawn patterns still benefit because allocations accumulate and trigger GC over time.
Visual: Pool as Queue
Pool
Queue<GameObject> holding inactive objects. Enqueue when returned, Dequeue when borrowed.
Example
Bullets: pre-allocate 20 bullets, reuse them during a burst fire scenario to avoid GC spikes.
Key takeaway
Use pools for frequently spawned short-lived objects to reduce memory churn and improve frame stability.

screens.title: Implementing a Simple Bullet Pool
screens.subtitle: A concrete Queue-based pool and the borrow/return API.

narration.text: Let's walk through a simple object pool implementation for bullets using a queue. The pool pre-instantiates a fixed number of bullet prefabs in Awake, sets them inactive, and enqueues them. The GetBullet method Dequeues an object, activates it, and hands it to the caller. If the pool is empty you can either expand the pool or log a warning. ReturnBullet deactivates the bullet and enqueues it again. This A P I keeps runtime code simple: instead of calling Instantiate or Destroy, gameplay code calls GetBullet and ReturnBullet. A common extension is to parent pooled objects to the pool object for tidy Hierarchy organization. A misconception to watch for is leaving object state intact: always reset position, velocity, timers, or component fields when you borrow an object. Below is the canonical code snippet from the chapter; study how Awake fills the queue and how GetBullet/ReturnBullet manage activation. After implementing, test by firing many bullets and compare Profiler traces with and without the pool. You should see fewer Instantiate calls and lower GC allocations during heavy firing. Implementing a Simple Bullet Pool means pre-instantiate objects in awake, borrow via get, return via return, and reset state when activating.. In practical terms, a concrete queue-based pool and the borrow/return api.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Implementation pattern
keyIdea.text: Pre-instantiate objects in Awake, borrow via Get, return via Return, and reset state when activating.

content.html:
Process Flow › Bullet Pool Code
Code example
// Simple Object Pool Example
public class BulletPool : MonoBehaviour
{
    public GameObject bulletPrefab;
    public int poolSize = 20;
    private Queue<GameObject> _bulletPool = new Queue<GameObject>();

    void Awake()
    {
        for (int i = 0; i < poolSize; i++)
        {
            GameObject bullet = Instantiate(bulletPrefab);
            bullet.SetActive(false);
            _bulletPool.Enqueue(bullet);
        }
    }

    public GameObject GetBullet()
    {
        if (_bulletPool.Count > 0)
        {
            GameObject bullet = _bulletPool.Dequeue();
            bullet.SetActive(true);
            return bullet;
        }
        else
        {
            Debug.LogWarning("Bullet pool exhausted, instantiating new bullet.");
            return Instantiate(bulletPrefab);
        }
    }

    public void ReturnBullet(GameObject bullet)
    {
        bullet.SetActive(false);
        _bulletPool.Enqueue(bullet);
    }
}
Walkthrough & tips
  • Pre-allocate in Awake to avoid runtime spikes.
  • Reset object state on enable: position, velocity, timers.
  • Decide whether to expand the pool or log a warning on exhaustion.
  • Parent pooled objects under the spawner for Hierarchy cleanliness.
Key Takeaway

Replace Instantiate/Destroy with Get/Return calls and reset state to prevent unexpected behavior and reduce allocations.

screens.title: Putting the Pool in a Scene (Singleton Spawner)
screens.subtitle: Steps to refactor a scene to use BulletSpawner with cached pool access.

narration.text: This slide guides a simple hands-on refactor: convert per-bullet Instantiate/Destroy behavior into a centralized BulletSpawner singleton that manages a pool. Start a new scene and create a Bullet prefab with a Rigidbody and a small script that moves forward and returns to the pool after its lifetime. Add an empty BulletSpawner GameObject and implement the pool in Awake, instantiating the bullets as children for organization. Turn the spawner into a singleton so any code can call BulletSpawner. Instance. GetBullet(). Replace direct Instantiate usage in firing code with GetBullet. In the bullet script, call BulletSpawner. Instance. ReturnBullet(gameObject) in place of Destroy. Test by rapidly firing while observing the Hierarchy: you should see a fixed number of pooled objects toggling active state rather than many new instances appearing and disappearing. Profile both versions: before refactor you'll observe Instantiate calls and higher GC allocations; after refactor you should see a reduced frequency of allocations and smoother frame timing. A common error is forgetting to reset velocities or timers when reusing objects; always restore initial state on enable. Reflection question: how did the Hierarchy and Profiler change after the swap?

keyIdea.title: Refactor steps
keyIdea.text: Create Bullet prefab, implement singleton spawner with pool, replace Instantiate/Destroy calls with Get/Return, and reset object state on enable.

Hands-on Activity › BulletSpawner Refactor
Step-by-step
  1. Create Bullet prefab with Rigidbody and Bullet script.
  2. Add BulletSpawner GameObject and implement pool in Awake.
  3. Make BulletSpawner a singleton for easy access.
  4. Replace Instantiate with GetBullet and Destroy with ReturnBullet.
  5. Test rapid fire and compare Profiler traces.
Example: Return in Bullet
void Update()
{
    transform.Translate(Vector3.forward * speed * Time.deltaTime);
    _currentLifetime -= Time.deltaTime;
    if (_currentLifetime <= 0)
    {
        BulletSpawner.Instance.ReturnBullet(gameObject); // Instead of Destroy
    }
}
Tip: Reset Rigidbody velocity and local position in OnEnable to avoid residual state when reusing a bullet.

screens.title: Instantiate/Destroy vs Object Pooling
screens.subtitle: Trade-offs and when to choose pooling.

narration.text: Comparing Instantiate/Destroy with pooling clarifies when to refactor. Instantiate and Destroy are simple and fine for rare allocations or editor tools, but they become problematic when many objects are created per second. Each Instantiate allocates memory and runs initialization code; each Destroy marks memory for reclamation, which eventually triggers the garbage collector. This pattern produces GC allocations that show up as periodic spikes in the Profiler. Object pooling trades a small upfront allocation cost for steady runtime behavior. Pools allocate once and then toggle objects active and inactive, avoiding repeated allocations. The trade-offs are clear: pooling adds complexity—managing pool size, reset logic, and potential leaks if objects aren't returned—but yields much lower runtime GC churn. A misconception is that pooling always reduces memory usage; a pool keeps memory allocated for the pool size, so peak memory may rise, but runtime allocation and GC frequency fall. Choose pooling when object spawn rate causes visible frame hitches or frequent Instantiate calls appear in the Profiler. Key question: is the runtime stability from fewer allocations worth the extra code complexity in this feature?

keyIdea.title: Trade-off
keyIdea.text: Pooling reduces runtime allocations and GC spikes at the cost of initial allocation and added management complexity.

content.html:
Comparison › Instantiate/Destroy vs Pooling
Instantiate / Destroy
  • Simple to implement.
  • Allocates memory per instance.
  • Causes GC work over time, producing spikes.
When this is ok
Use for rare or editor-only creation where performance is not critical.
Object Pooling
  • Pre-allocates objects once.
  • Reuses objects to avoid allocations.
  • Requires reset logic and pool management.
When this is recommended
Use when spawn rate is high or Profiler shows repeated Instantiate calls and GC spikes during gameplay.
Practical question

Does your gameplay create many short-lived objects per second? If yes, prefer pooling to keep frame times stable.

screens.title: Minimizing Garbage Collection Allocations
screens.subtitle: Recognize common allocation sources and practical alternatives.

narration.text: Minimizing garbage collection allocations starts with identifying what creates garbage. Common culprits include string concatenations performed every frame, implicit boxing when passing value types to APIs expecting object, LINQ queries that allocate temporary enumerables and delegates, creating new collections within hot loops, and coroutines or A P I calls that allocate helper objects each time. For strings, avoid building them every frame; use cached StringBuilder for heavy concatenation or minimize concatenation in Update. For boxing, be mindful when passing ints or structs into methods that accept object; prefer overloads or explicit formatting that avoids boxing. LINQ is expressive but can allocate; avoid LINQ in hot paths or cache its results. New arrays and lists inside Update should be replaced by reused buffers or cleared lists. Coroutines that yield new WaitForSeconds each time should instead reuse a cached WaitForSeconds instance. Lastly, Unity APIs that return arrays or lists on each call are often available in overloads that accept a preallocated List or array to fill; prefer those to avoid per-call allocations. A practical approach is to run the Profiler, find the objects or allocations under GC Alloc, and then refactor the exact lines causing allocations, measure again, and repeat until allocations are acceptable.

keyIdea.title: Allocation sources
keyIdea.text: Strings, boxing, LINQ, new collections, coroutines, and some Unity API overloads are frequent sources of runtime allocations.

content.html:
Core Concept › Minimizing GC
Common pitfalls
  • String concatenation every frame instead of reusing builders.
  • Boxing when value types are passed to object parameters, including some Debug calls.
  • LINQ queries and closures generating temporary allocations in hot paths.
  • Allocating new collections or arrays inside Update loops.
  • Creating new WaitForSeconds instances per coroutine yield.
Quick remedies
  • Cache StringBuilder and reuse it.
  • Use overloads that avoid object parameters and boxing.
  • Cache LINQ results or avoid LINQ in Update.
  • Reuse lists/arrays and clear them instead of creating new ones.
  • Cache WaitForSeconds instances for repeated yields.
Key Takeaway

Find allocation hotspots with the Profiler and apply targeted refactors: caching, pooling, or replacing allocation-heavy APIs.

screens.title: Concrete Refactors: WaitForSeconds & String Handling
screens.subtitle: Code examples that remove common per-frame allocations.

narration.text: Two compact, high-impact refactors are caching WaitForSeconds in coroutines and avoiding repeated string allocations. In the bad coroutine example, returning new WaitForSeconds(1f) each loop creates a fresh object every iteration. By caching a private WaitForSeconds field and reusing it, you eliminate those allocations. For strings, avoid concatenating many parts every frame; repeated string assembly produces many short-lived string objects. Use a reused StringBuilder for heavy building, or limit per-frame string work by updating UI only when the displayed value changes. Another frequent mistake is calling Debug. Log with value types repeatedly, which can cause boxing and string creation. Remove or gate debug logging in hot paths or use conditional compilation. Below are the two code examples: first shows the bad and good coroutine pattern; second provides a pattern for caching a StringBuilder or reducing per-frame string work. After making these changes re-run the Profiler and expect reduced GC allocation rate and fewer small temporary objects in the allocation timeline. Concrete Refactors: WaitForSeconds & String Handling means cache waitforseconds and avoid per-frame string rebuilding to prevent frequent small allocations.. In practical terms, code examples that remove common per-frame allocations.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Refactor patterns
keyIdea.text: Cache WaitForSeconds and avoid per-frame string rebuilding to prevent frequent small allocations.

content.html:
Definition › No-allocation code patterns
Coroutine: Bad vs Good
// BAD: Allocates new WaitForSeconds every loop
IEnumerator MyCoroutineBad()
{
    while (true)
    {
        yield return new WaitForSeconds(1f);
        // ...
    }
}

// GOOD: Cache WaitForSeconds
private WaitForSeconds _oneSecondWait = new WaitForSeconds(1f);
IEnumerator MyCoroutineGood()
{
    while (true)
    {
        yield return _oneSecondWait;
        // ...
    }
}
String handling pattern
// BAD: Concatenate every frame
void Update()
{
    scoreText.text = "Score: " + playerScore + " - Lives: " + lives;
}

// BETTER: Update only when values change
private int _lastScore = -1;
void UpdateScoreUI()
{
    if (_lastScore != playerScore)
    {
        _lastScore = playerScore;
        scoreText.text = $"Score: {playerScore} - Lives: {lives}";
    }
}
Measure after these refactors. Removing repeated allocations in hot paths yields visible drops in GC allocation rate and fewer small-object allocations on the Profiler timeline.

screens.title: Optimize Update() and FixedUpdate() Loops
screens.subtitle: Caching, early exits, and reducing frequency to save per-frame CPU.

narration.text: Update and FixedUpdate run predictably: Update every frame, FixedUpdate at a fixed timestep for physics. Because they run so often, even small inefficiencies multiply. First rule: cache component references in Awake or Start; calling GetComponent every frame is expensive. Second, ask if the work really needs to run every frame. Many calculations, like pathfinding or expensive AI decisions, can be run every 0.2–0.5 seconds or on demand via events. Use timers or coroutines with cached WaitForSeconds instances to spread workload across frames. Third, use early exits: guard the method with a simple condition and return early if work isn't needed. This avoids unnecessary allocations and calculations. Fourth, switch to event-driven patterns where possible so code reacts to state changes rather than polling. For physics in FixedUpdate, keep logic minimal and perform non-physics updates in Update. A common misconception is that more frequent updates always look smoother; often responsiveness is preserved while shifting heavy processing to less frequent intervals, improving frame stability. Concrete example: cache Rigidbody in Awake and call AddForce in Update without GetComponent every frame. Measure Scripts time before and after to confirm savings.

keyIdea.title: Update best practices
keyIdea.text: Cache references, use early exits, lower update frequency, and prefer events to polling to reduce per-frame cost.

content.html:
Process Flow › Update / FixedUpdate
Practical rules
  • Cache GetComponent results in Awake or Start.
  • Use early return patterns to skip work when not needed.
  • Reduce frequency with timers or coroutines for noncritical tasks.
  • Move heavy work off Update; use events to trigger work only when necessary.
Example refactor
// BAD
void Update()
{
    Rigidbody rb = GetComponent<Rigidbody>();
    rb.AddForce(Vector3.forward);
}

// GOOD
private Rigidbody _rb;
void Awake() { _rb = GetComponent<Rigidbody>(); }
void Update()
{
    if (!_isActive) return; // early exit
    _rb.AddForce(Vector3.forward);
}
Why it matters

Small per-frame costs add up. Caching and frequency reduction are simple changes that produce large runtime savings.

screens.title: Efficient Use of Unity API Calls
screens.subtitle: Which Unity calls are expensive and how to avoid them.

narration.text: Some Unity A P I calls are deceptively expensive because they perform scene-wide searches or allocate memory. Camera. main, for example, can call FindObjectOfType under the hood unless cached; calling Camera. main repeatedly each frame is therefore costly. GetComponent, GameObject. Find, and FindObjectOfType scan for components or game objects and should not be used in Update. Debug. Log can cause boxing and string allocation, so frequent logging in hot paths hurts performance. Physics queries that allocate arrays or lists, like certain overloads of OverlapSphere or GetComponents without a preallocated list, produce allocations; prefer overloads that accept a pre-filled List or array to avoid per-call allocation. Use SerializeField and assign references in the Inspector when possible, or cache references in Awake/Start. When you must locate objects at runtime, do it once and cache the result. A practical architecture is to centralize frequently used references in manager objects that expose cached fields. A misconception is that these calls are micro-optimizations; in aggregate during gameplay they often dominate Scripts time. The correct pattern is to favor direct references and cached access, and to profile before and after changes to confirm impact.

keyIdea.title: API cost awareness
keyIdea.text: Cache expensive Unity API results and prefer preallocated overloads to minimize both search cost and allocations.

content.html:
Architecture › Unity API Efficiency
Expensive calls to avoid in hot paths
  • Camera.main (cache in Awake if used often)
  • GetComponent<T> inside Update (cache once)
  • GameObject.Find and FindObjectOfType (expensive scene-wide searches)
  • Debug.Log with value types in tight loops (boxing + string allocations)
  • API overloads that return new arrays/lists each call
Architectural patterns
  • Use SerializeField to assign references in the Inspector.
  • Centralize frequently accessed objects in managers and cache them.
  • Prefer API overloads that accept preallocated collections.
Action

Audit your project for repeated API calls in Update and replace them with cached references or inspector-assigned fields.

screens.title: Data Structures & Algorithms for Unity
screens.subtitle: Choose structures that match access patterns to reduce CPU time.

narration.text: Choosing the right data structure and algorithm matters in game code as much as in general software. Lists are flexible and fast for iteration and small collections, while queues and stacks naturally express FIFO and LIFO patterns like pools and undo histories. Dictionaries provide constant-time lookup when you need keyed access; prefer them over linear searches when you repeatedly query by ID or name. Arrays are the most compact and fastest for indexed access and should be used when collection size is fixed or known. A common mistake is using LINQ to query collections in Update every frame; that introduces both C P U overhead and allocations. Similarly, repeatedly sorting a list inside Update is expensive; instead maintain lists in sorted order when possible or only sort when data changes. Algorithmic choices—such as O(n) scan versus O(1) dictionary lookup—have practical implications. If your code polls dozens or hundreds of objects each frame, prefer spatial partitioning or cached structures that limit iteration. The practical guidance: match collection type to access pattern, avoid per-frame allocations from new collections, and measure both C P U time and allocation counts to guide changes.

keyIdea.title: Structure selection
keyIdea.text: Pick arrays, lists, queues, or dictionaries based on access and update patterns to minimize iteration and lookup costs.

content.html:
Hierarchy › Data Structures
Arrays
Best for fixed-size collections and fastest indexed access. Low overhead and cache-friendly.
List<T>
Flexible, good for iteration. Avoid creating new lists in Update; clear and reuse existing lists instead.
Dictionary<K,V>
Use for constant-time lookups when repeated queries by key occur each frame.
Tip
Avoid per-frame sorting and LINQ queries in hot paths. Maintain order when possible or run heavy operations on changes only.
Why it matters
Algorithmic complexity directly affects frame cost when operations run every frame. Choose structures to limit per-frame work.

screens.title: Cache GetComponent & Measure Profiler Impact
screens.subtitle: Refactor a PlayerMovement script and compare CPU cost.

narration.text: A clear demonstration of caching is the PlayerMovement example. In the bad example, GetComponent is called inside Update, creating repeated lookup cost. The correct pattern is to cache the Rigidbody reference in Awake and use the cached field in Update. After making this change, profile the scene and inspect 'Scripts' time: you should observe a measurable drop in C P U cost for that component. The hands-on activity in the chapter instructs you to first implement the bad PlayerMovement on a Capsule with Rigidbody and profile it. Then refactor to cache the Rigidbody in Awake and re-profile. The practical measurement is the difference in C P U time attributed to the PlayerMovement. Update method. A misconception is expecting a dramatic single-frame change; in many cases the improvement is modest per-frame but meaningful when multiplied across many components or many frames. Also remember to remove extraneous Debug. Log calls in Update as they can overshadow the effect of caching. After verifying the results, apply the same caching pattern to other frequently polled components in your project to compound the benefit. Cache GetComponent & Measure Profiler Impact means cache getcomponent in awake, re-run the profiler, and confirm reduced scripts time for per-frame logic.. In practical terms, refactor a playermovement script and compare cpu cost.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Measure caching
keyIdea.text: Cache GetComponent in Awake, re-run the Profiler, and confirm reduced Scripts time for per-frame logic.

content.html:
Refactor Example › Caching GetComponent
BAD: GetComponent every frame
// PlayerMovement.cs (BAD EXAMPLE)
using UnityEngine;

public class PlayerMovement : MonoBehaviour
{
    public float moveSpeed = 5f;

    void Update()
    {
        Rigidbody rb = GetComponent<Rigidbody>();
        if (rb != null)
        {
            float horizontal = Input.GetAxis("Horizontal");
            float vertical = Input.GetAxis("Vertical");
            Vector3 moveDirection = new Vector3(horizontal, 0, vertical).normalized;
            rb.velocity = moveDirection * moveSpeed;
        }
    }
}
GOOD: Cache in Awake
// PlayerMovement.cs (GOOD EXAMPLE)
using UnityEngine;

public class PlayerMovement : MonoBehaviour
{
    public float moveSpeed = 5f;
    private Rigidbody _rb; // Cached reference

    void Awake()
    {
        _rb = GetComponent<Rigidbody>(); // Get once
    }

    void Update()
    {
        if (_rb != null)
        {
            float horizontal = Input.GetAxis("Horizontal");
            float vertical = Input.GetAxis("Vertical");
            Vector3 moveDirection = new Vector3(horizontal, 0, vertical).normalized;
            _rb.velocity = moveDirection * moveSpeed;
        }
    }
}
After refactor, use the Profiler to compare CPU time for the Update function and confirm the reduction. Apply this pattern broadly for repeated lookups.

narration.text: Review these core concepts as quick anchors for optimization work. Object Pooling prevents frequent allocation by reusing objects; it is the principal pattern for high-spawn scenarios. Garbage Collection is the automatic memory reclamation system; frequent allocations force more GC runs and cause frame hitches. Memory Allocation is the act of reserving memory for an object; minimizing allocations in hot paths reduces GC pressure. Each of these is linked: object pooling reduces allocations, which lowers GC work and stabilizes frame time. Keep these concepts in mind while profiling and refactoring, and use the verified milestones earlier in the lesson to confirm improvements in the Profiler. What to Remember › Key Concepts
Object Pooling
Pre-allocate and reuse objects to cut allocations and GC overhead.
Garbage Collection
Automatic memory reclamation that can cause noticeable pauses when it runs frequently.
Memory Allocation
Reserve memory for objects. Minimize allocations in hot paths to reduce GC runs.
Summary

Use pooling, reduce per-frame allocations, and cache expensive API calls to stabilize frame time and improve runtime experience.

narration.text: These practical reminders help you act on what you learned. Caching References means storing component or camera references in Awake or Start to avoid repeated lookups. GetComponent and Find methods are inexpensive occasionally but expensive when used every frame; cache their results. Update vs FixedUpdate: place physics-related code in FixedUpdate and minimize work in both methods, favoring events where possible. Get comfortable with the Profiler: identify GC Alloc spikes and the Scripts time, then map those to code and refactor specifically. A useful habit is small, measurable changes: fix one allocation source, reprofile, then move to the next. This iterative approach helps you prioritize the highest-impact refactors and avoid unnecessary complexity.
